paragraphs: Fire is now set to the ship of Protesilaus, and Patroclus goes into battle in the armor of Achilles—He pushes the Trojans back, but in the end Euphorbus and Hector kill him.

So the fight went on around the ship of Protesilaus. Meanwhile Patroclus came up to Achilles with tears welling in his eyes, like a spring whose dark water spills down the ledges of a high cliff. Achilles saw him crying and felt sorry for him. He said, “Patroclus, why are you standing there in tears like a silly little girl who runs to her mother and begs to be picked up and carried? She clings to her mother’s dress and holds her back though her mother is in a hurry, and she keeps looking up at her with wet eyes until her mother lifts her. You are shedding tears just like that, Patroclus. Do you have something to tell the Myrmidons, or me? Or have you had news from Phthia that only you know? They tell me that Menoetius son of Actor is still alive, and that Peleus son of Aeacus is still alive among the Myrmidons. We two would grieve bitterly to lose either of them. Or are you mourning for the Argives, and for the way they are being killed at the ships because of their own arrogance? Do not hide anything from me. Say it, so that both of us know.”

Then, knight Patroclus, you answered with a deep sigh, “Achilles, son of Peleus, greatest champion of the Achaeans, do not be angry. I weep because of the disaster that has fallen on the Argives. Every man who has been their champion until now is lying at the ships, wounded by sword or spear. Brave Diomedes son of Tydeus has been hit by a spear. Famed Odysseus and Agamemnon have both taken sword wounds. Eurypylus has been struck in the thigh by an arrow. Skilled healers are tending these heroes and curing their wounds. And you, Achilles, are you still so unyielding? May I never carry the kind of rage you carry, to the ruin of your own good name. Who in later stories will speak well of you if you do not save the Argives from destruction now? You have no pity. The knight Peleus was not your father, and Thetis was not your mother. The gray sea bore you and the sheer cliffs gave you life, you are so cruel and hard. But perhaps you are holding back because you know of some oracle, or because your mother Thetis has told you something from the mouth of Zeus. If so, at least send me out, and the Myrmidons with me, in case I can bring the Danaans some relief. And let me wear your armor. The Trojans may take me for you and leave the field, and the hard-pressed sons of the Achaeans can get a chance to breathe. They have hardly had one while fighting. We are fresh, and we could easily drive these tired men back from our ships and tents to their own city.”

He did not know what he was asking, or that he was begging for his own death. Achilles was deeply moved, and he answered, “Noble Patroclus, what are you saying? I am not heeding any prophecy that I know of, and my mother has told me nothing from the mouth of Zeus. What cuts me to the heart is that a man of my own rank should dare to rob me, only because he has more power than I do. After everything I have been through, it is more than I can bear. The girl the sons of the Achaeans picked out for me, whom I won with my spear when I sacked a city—King Agamemnon took her from me as if I were some common vagrant. Still, let bygones be bygones. No man can keep his anger forever. I said I would not give way until the battle and the war cry reached my own ships. But now, strap my armor around your shoulders and lead the Myrmidons into the fight. The dark cloud of Trojans has burst furiously over our fleet. The Argives are pushed back onto the beach and penned into a narrow space, and the whole people of Troy has grown bold enough to come out against them, because they do not see the visor of my helmet gleaming close by. If they had seen it, they would have fled, and there would not be a creek or gully that was not filled with their dead. That is how it would have gone, if only King Agamemnon had treated me fairly. As things are, the Trojans have surrounded our army. Diomedes son of Tydeus no longer wields his spear to defend the Danaans, and I have not heard the voice of the son of Atreus coming from his hated head. What rings in my ears is the voice of murderous Hector giving orders to the Trojans, who triumph over the Achaeans and fill the whole plain with their battle cry. But even so, Patroclus, fall on them and save the fleet, or the Trojans will burn it and cut off our way home. Do exactly as I now tell you, so that you win me great honor from all the Danaans, and they give the girl back to me with splendid gifts besides. When you have driven the Trojans from the ships, come back. Even if Hera’s thundering husband puts victory within your reach, do not fight the Trojans further without me, or you will rob me of glory that should be mine. And do not let your lust for battle carry you into killing more Trojans, or leading the Achaeans on toward Ilium. One of the ever-living gods may come down from Olympus and attack you, for Phoebus Apollo loves the Trojans well. Return once you have freed the ships from danger, and let others fight on the plain. By father Zeus, Athena and Apollo, I wish that not one Trojan were left alive, and not one Argive either, and that only we two were left to tear off the veil that covers the brow of Troy.”

So they spoke together. Meanwhile Ajax could no longer hold his ground under the shower of darts that rained on him. The will of Zeus and the Trojan javelins were too much for him. The helmet gleaming at his temples rang without pause as the missiles kept pouring onto it and onto the cheek-pieces that guarded his face. His left shoulder was also worn out from holding his shield so long. Still, however hard they threw at him, they could not make him give way. He could hardly breathe. Sweat ran from every pore of his body. He had not a moment’s rest, and danger upon danger pressed on him from every side.

And now, Muses who have your homes on Olympus, tell me how fire was thrown on the ships of the Achaeans. Hector came up close and swung his great sword at the ashen spear of Ajax. He cut it clean in two, just behind the place where the point was fixed to the shaft. So Ajax was left holding a headless spear, while the bronze point flew off some distance and landed ringing on the ground. Ajax saw the hand of heaven in this. He was dismayed to see that Zeus had left him completely defenseless and wanted the Trojans to win. So he drew back, and the Trojans hurled fire at the ship, which at once was wrapped in flames.

The fire was now blazing around the ship’s stern. Achilles slapped his two thighs and said to Patroclus, “Up, noble knight! I can see the glare of enemy fire at our fleet. Up, before they destroy our ships and leave us no way to retreat. Put on your armor at once while I call our people together.”

As he spoke, Patroclus began to arm. First he strapped greaves of good make on his legs, fitted with silver ankle-clasps. After that he put on the cuirass of the son of Aeacus, richly inlaid and studded. He hung his silver-studded sword of bronze from his shoulders, and then took up his mighty shield. On his handsome head he set the well-made helmet, with its crest of horse-hair nodding threateningly above. He took two sturdy spears that fitted his hands. But he did not take the spear of noble Achilles, so stout and strong, because no other Achaean could wield it, though Achilles handled it easily. It was an ashen spear from Mount Pelion. Chiron had cut it on a mountain top and given it to Peleus, to deal out death among heroes. Patroclus told Automedon to yoke the horses quickly. Next to Achilles, Automedon was the man he honored most, and the one he could most firmly rely on in battle. So Automedon yoked the swift horses Xanthus and Balius, who could fly like the wind. The harpy Podarge had borne them to the west wind as she grazed in a meadow by the waters of the river Oceanus. In the side traces he set the noble horse Pedasus. Achilles had taken him away when he sacked the city of Eetion, and though Pedasus was a mortal horse, he could keep pace with the immortal ones.

Meanwhile Achilles went everywhere among the tents and told his Myrmidons to put on their armor. Think of fierce, ravening wolves feasting on a horned stag they have killed in the mountains, their jaws red with blood. They go in a pack to lap water from a clear spring with their long thin tongues, and they reek of blood and slaughter. They do not know what fear is, because hunger drives them. In the same way the leaders and counselors of the Myrmidons gathered around the good squire of the swift descendant of Aeacus, and Achilles himself stood among them, urging on both men and horses.

Noble Achilles had brought fifty ships to Troy, and each had a crew of fifty oarsmen. Over them he set five captains he could trust, and he himself commanded them all. Menesthius of the gleaming corslet led the first company. He was the son of the river Spercheius, which streams down from heaven. Fair Polydora, daughter of Peleus, had borne him to ever-flowing Spercheius—a woman joined to a god. But he was called the son of Borus son of Perieres, who lived with his mother as her husband, and who had given great wealth to win her. Noble Eudorus, the son of an unmarried woman, led the second company. Polymele, daughter of Phylas the graceful dancer, bore him. The mighty slayer of Argus had fallen in love with her when he saw her among the singing women at a dance in honor of Artemis, the rushing huntress of the golden arrows. So Hermes, giver of all good, went up with her to an upper chamber and lay with her in secret. She bore him a noble son, Eudorus, who was singularly swift-footed and valiant in a fight. Ilithuia, goddess of the pains of childbirth, brought him into the light, and he saw the face of the sun. Then mighty Echecles son of Actor took the mother as his wife, giving great wealth to win her. Her father Phylas brought the child up and cared for him, doting on him as fondly as if he were his own son. Pisander son of Maemalus led the third company. Among all the Myrmidons he was the finest spearman, after Achilles’s own comrade Patroclus. The old knight Phoenix was captain of the fourth company, and Alcimedon, noble son of Laerceus, of the fifth.

When Achilles had chosen his men and stationed them all with their captains, he gave them a stern charge. “Myrmidons,” he said, “remember the threats you made against the Trojans at the ships, in the time of my anger, when you were all complaining of me. ‘Cruel son of Peleus,’ you would say, ‘your mother must have fed you on gall, you are so ruthless. You keep us here at the ships against our will. If you are going to be this relentless, we had better go home over the sea.’ Often you have gathered and scolded me like that. Now the hour has come for the great feats of arms you have so long been longing for. So let every one of you keep a high heart to do battle with the Trojans.”

With these words he put heart and soul into every man, and when they heard their king’s words they closed their companies up even tighter. As a builder fits stones tightly into the wall of a high house that must give shelter from the winds, so closely were the helmets and bossed shields set against one another. Shield pressed on shield, helm on helm, and man on man. They stood so close that the horse-hair plumes on the gleaming ridges of their helmets touched as they bent their heads.

In front of them all, two men armed themselves—Patroclus and Automedon—two men with one mind, to lead the Myrmidons. Then Achilles went into his tent and opened the lid of the strong chest that silver-footed Thetis had given him to take on board ship, and had filled with shirts, cloaks against the cold, and good thick rugs. In this chest he kept a cup of rare workmanship. No man but himself might drink from it, and he made offerings from it to no god except father Zeus. He took the cup from the chest and cleansed it with sulphur. Then he rinsed it in clean water, washed his hands, and drew wine. He stood in the middle of the court and prayed, looking toward heaven and pouring out the wine as a drink offering. Zeus, whose joy is in thunder, did not fail to see him. “King Zeus,” he cried, “lord of Dodona, god of the Pelasgi, you who live far away and rule wintry Dodona, where your prophets the Selli live around you with unwashed feet and beds made on the ground—you heard me when I prayed to you before, and honored me by sending disaster on the Achaeans. Now grant me the fulfilment of one more prayer. I will stay here where my ships are lying, but I am sending my comrade into battle at the head of many Myrmidons. Grant, all-seeing Zeus, that victory goes with him. Put your courage into his heart, so that Hector learns whether my squire is man enough to fight alone, or whether his might is unbeatable only when I myself enter the turmoil of war. Afterward, when he has driven the fighting and the battle cry away from the ships, grant that he returns unharmed, with his armor and his comrades, fighters in close combat.”

So he prayed, and all-counselling Zeus heard his prayer. He granted part of it, but not all. He agreed that Patroclus would thrust war and battle back from the ships, but he refused to let him come out of the fight safely.
When Achilles had poured his drink offering and prayed, he went back into his tent and put the cup away in his chest.
Then he came out again, because he still loved to watch the fierce fight raging between the Trojans and Achaeans.

Meanwhile the armed band around Patroclus marched on until they sprang at the Trojans, high in hope. They swarmed out like wasps whose nests are by the roadside, and which silly children love to tease, so that anyone passing by may get stung. Or again, if a traveler on the road annoys them by accident, every wasp comes flying out in a fury to defend its young. With that same rage and courage the Myrmidons swarmed from their ships, and their battle cry rose to the heavens. Patroclus called to his men at the top of his voice, “Myrmidons, followers of Achilles son of Peleus, be men, my friends! Fight with all your might and main, so that we win glory for the son of Peleus, who is by far the foremost man at the ships of the Argives—he and his close-fighting followers. Then King Agamemnon, son of Atreus, will learn his folly in showing no respect to the bravest of the Achaeans.”

With these words he put heart and soul into every man, and they fell on the Trojans in a body. The ships rang again with the cry the Achaeans raised. When the Trojans saw the brave son of Menoetius and his squire, both gleaming in their armor, they lost heart and their battalions fell into confusion. They thought the swift son of Peleus must have put aside his anger and made peace with Agamemnon. Every man looked around to see where he could flee to safety.

Patroclus was the first to aim a spear. He threw it into the middle of the crowd, where men were packed most thickly, by the stern of the ship of Protesilaus. He hit Pyraechmes, who had led his Paeonian horsemen from Amydon and the broad waters of the river Axius. The spear struck him in the right shoulder and he fell backward in the dust with a groan. His men fell into confusion, because by killing their leader, the finest soldier among them, Patroclus had struck panic into them all. So he drove them away from the ship and put out the fire that was blazing there, leaving the half-burnt ship where it lay. The Trojans were driven back with a shout that split the skies, and the Danaans poured after them from their ships, shouting just as ceaselessly. As when Zeus, gatherer of the thunder cloud, spreads a dense canopy over the top of a lofty mountain, and all the peaks, the jutting headlands and the forest glades show out in the great light flashing from the bursting heavens, so the Danaans, having driven the fire back from their ships, took a short breath. But the fury of the fight was not over. The Trojans had not been driven back in utter rout. They still gave battle, and were forced from their ground only by sheer fighting.
